content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler green beans, Stage 2 are gently cooked snap beans designed for children aged 8 to 12 months. They are rich in vitamins, minerals, and dietary fiber, and have a mild flavor that is easily accepted by small stomachs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green beans are one of the first vegetables introduced to infants as purees or finely chopped pieces.
The beans provide plant protein that supports growth and tissue development.
In Stage 2 the beans are partially softened but retain small pieces to develop chewing skills.
Green beans are high in folate, important for nervous system development in babies.
They contain antioxidants that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and enhances iron absorption from plant foods.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is essential for proper nervous system development and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps establish a beneficial gut microbiome.

items.title: Low in sodium
items.content: Low sodium levels make the product safe for a developing infant who is not ready for high salt intake.

items.title: Plant protein
items.content: Protein from beans supports muscle growth and tissue development in toddlers.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some children may develop an allergy to legumes; monitor for reactions when first introduced.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Bean pieces should be soft and finely cut to prevent choking in children under 12 months.

items.title: Food contamination
items.content: Product must be stored in a sealed package and be heat‑treated to eliminate bacterial risks.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Green beans contain small amounts of oxalates; children prone to kidney stones should have limited intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the beans as soft pieces or puree mixed with breast milk, infant formula, or a small amount of vegetable broth. For beginners, mash the beans with a fork before offering.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator and use within 3 days.

chicken-leg-drumstick-and-thigh-stewed-s.title: Chicken leg, drumstick and thigh, stewed, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed chicken parts – leg, drumstick and thigh – are pieces of meat with skin cooked by slow simmering in liquid. This method makes the meat tender while the skin becomes flavorful and slightly crisp. The product is commonly used in stews, soups, or served as a main dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken legs and thighs contain more connective tissue than breast meat, making them ideal for long cooking.
Stewed skin retains some of its fat, giving the dish a rich taste.
In many traditional cuisines (e.g., Russian, Polish, American) stewed chicken parts are considered classic comfort food.
When cooked properly the meat stays juicy and the skin can become lightly crisp if finished with a quick sear.
Stewed chicken pieces are often added to broths to deepen flavor.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken meat provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Stewed parts are a source of vitamin B6 and niacin, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: The product supplies iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood formation, immunity and bone health.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and skin fat helps keep you feeling full for longer.

items.title: Contains collagen
items.content: Skin‑on chicken retains collagen, which may benefit skin elasticity and joint health.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Chicken parts with skin are richer in fat, so portion control is advisable for those watching calorie intake.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improper cooking can leave pathogens (e.g., Salmonella) alive. Ensure internal temperature reaches at least 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium in prepared dishes
items.content: Stewed products made with added salt or sauces can be high in sodium.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stewed legs, drumsticks and thighs can be served as a standalone portion, added to soups, stews, salads, or used in sandwiches. The skin can be eaten together with the meat or briefly pan‑fried for extra crispness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked product in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in sealed bags at –18 °C (0 °F) where it retains quality for 2‑3 months. Reheat thoroughly before consumption.

chicken-thigh-baked-broiled-or-roasted-s.title: Chicken thigh, baked, broiled, or roasted, skin eaten, from raw

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken thigh is the meat taken from the upper part of a bird's leg. When baked, broiled, or roasted, the skin is often left on, adding moisture and flavor. Thigh meat is rich in protein, iron, zinc, and B‑vitamins, especially B12.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thighs contain more fat than chicken breast, making them juicier when cooked.
The skin helps retain moisture, resulting in a more succulent dish.
Various world cuisines (American, Mediterranean, Asian) favor thighs for grilling and roasting.
Properly crisped skin is considered a delicacy in many cultures.
Chicken thighs are a common ingredient in stews, curries, and barbecue sauces.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Thighs provide about 20‑25 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nerve function and red blood cell formation, while niacin (B3) aids metabolism.

items.title: Minerals: iron and zinc
items.content: Iron is essential for oxygen transport, and zinc is important for immunity and wound healing.

items.title: Beneficial fats in the skin
items.content: The skin contains monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that, in moderation, support heart health.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat promotes lasting fullness.

items.title: Higher fat content
items.content: Thighs are more calorie‑dense than breast meat; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Chicken must be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 74 °C to eliminate salmonella.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: Sodium in prepared dishes
items.content: Pre‑marinated or sauced thighs can contain high levels of salt.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Thighs can be baked at 180‑200 °C for 30‑40 minutes, grilled, or pan‑seared until the skin is golden and crisp. The skin may be left on for texture or removed after cooking. Serve with vegetables, potatoes, rice, or slice into salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh chicken thighs keep in the refrigerator at +2‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen thighs last up to 12 months at ‑18 °C. Thaw in the fridge, not at room temperature, before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: The Cuban sandwich is a hot pressed sandwich made with roasted pork, ham, Swiss cheese, pickles, and mustard, layered between two slices of Cuban bread and grilled until the crust is golden and the cheese melts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sandwich originated in the early 1900s in Florida, where many Cuban immigrants settled.
Traditional bread is Cuban "pan cubano," slightly sweet and crisp on the outside.
The classic recipe uses only Swiss cheese, though some variations add mozzarella.
Cuban sandwiches are often served with French fries and pickled vegetables.
In 2015 the Cuban sandwich was listed among the "100 Best Foods in America" by Food & Wine.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Roast pork and ham provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Swiss cheese supplies calcium that supports bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and bread deliver B12 and other B‑vitamins important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotics from pickles
items.content: Fermented pickles contain live cultures that can benefit gut health.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: The traditional recipe contains little added sugar, keeping the sandwich moderately sweet.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Ham and pickles can be salty, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Pork and cheese are rich in saturated fats, which should be limited in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Swiss cheese may trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A Cuban sandwich is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sandwich hot, cut in half. It can be eaten with hands, or with a knife and fork if preferred. Optional toppings include chipotle sauce or a dash of hot sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The sandwich is best enjoyed immediately. Leftovers can be wrapped in foil and refrigerated for up to 24 hours, then reheated in an oven or on a grill.

content.title: About
content.content: The Double Cheeseburger is a classic fast‑food item consisting of two medium beef patties, two slices of cheese, a bun, lettuce, tomato, pickles, onion and sauce. It delivers a rich meat flavor, creamy cheese aroma and a crunchy vegetable texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The Double Cheeseburger entered major fast‑food menus in the early 1990s.
Each medium patty weighs about 80 g, totaling roughly 160 g of meat.
Two slices of processed cheese add up to about 150 mg of calcium per serving.
The burger is often served with fries and a soft drink as a combo meal.
Some regions offer variations with bacon or barbecue sauce.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The beef patties provide approximately 20 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and cheese supply B12, B6 and niacin, aiding energy metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The burger provides roughly 500–600 kcal, quickly replenishing energy stores.

items.title: High calorie and fat content
items.content: The large amount of saturated fat and calories can contribute to weight gain if consumed frequently.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Sauces and cheese can add significant salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Meat quality concerns
items.content: High‑temperature cooking can produce potentially harmful compounds such as acrylamide.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The burger is typically eaten by hand, holding the bottom bun. It can be customized with extra sauce, added bacon, or a whole‑grain bun for a healthier twist.

content.title: Storage
content.content: A prepared Double Cheeseburger should be refrigerated and consumed within 24 hours. For longer storage, freeze it and reheat in an oven or microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Mountain Dew AMP is an energy drink produced by PepsiCo. It contains caffeine, taurine, B‑vitamins, and sugar, delivering a quick boost of energy and heightened focus. The flavor blends citrus notes with a mild sweetness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: AMP was first launched in 2001 as a response to the growing energy‑drink market.
The drink provides about 32 mg of caffeine per 100 ml, roughly 80 mg in a standard 250 ml can.
The brand frequently partners with esports teams and music festivals.
In some countries the formula is altered to reduce sugar and add artificial sweeteners.
Packaging often features bright neon colors to emphasize its high‑energy image.

items.title: Increased alertness
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, improving attention and reaction time.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: B‑vitamins (B3, B6, B12) play key roles in cellular energy metabolism.

items.title: Enhanced physical endurance
items.content: Taurine may help muscles use energy more efficiently.

items.title: Excessive caffeine intake
items.content: High doses can cause anxiety, insomnia, and rapid heart rate.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Regular consumption may contribute to weight gain and elevated blood glucose.

items.title: Not recommended for children and pregnant women
items.content: Due to the high level of stimulants, these groups should limit consumption.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Drink AMP chilled, straight from the can. It is recommended not to exceed one 250 ml can within a 4‑hour period. Do not mix with alcohol.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 24 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Fajita is a Mexican dish consisting of thinly sliced beef or pork quickly seared on high heat with onions, bell peppers, and spices. The meat stays juicy while the vegetables become aromatic and slightly charred. It is usually served with tortillas, salsa, guacamole, and sour cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “fajita” comes from the Spanish “faja,” meaning “strip,” originally referring to strips of skirt steak.
Traditionally fajitas were made with skirt steak, but today pork, chicken, and even seafood are common alternatives.
The dish gained popularity in the United States in the 1970s thanks to the Taco Bell chain.
Authentic flavor often includes cumin, paprika, oregano, chili powder, and lime juice.
Fajitas are typically served “build‑your‑own,” letting each guest assemble the tortilla to taste.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef and pork provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat is abundant in B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Fajita supplies iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood formation, immunity, and bone health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: When served without sugary sauces, fajitas fit well into low‑carb diets.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Onions and bell peppers add vitamin C and carotenoids that help protect cells.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Pork and beef can contain saturated fats; choosing lean cuts and moderate portions is advisable.

items.title: Risk of over‑eating
items.content: The dish is often accompanied by tortillas and sauces, which can increase total calories if consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to chili, cumin, or other spices used in the marinade.

items.title: Food‑borne contamination
items.content: Meat must be fully cooked to avoid bacterial infections.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fajita in warm tortillas, adding salsa, guacamole, sour cream, shredded cheese, and fresh cilantro. It can also be used as a filling for burritos, tacos, or salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw meat in the refrigerator for up to 2 days; cooked fajita can be stored in an airtight container for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags for up to 3 months. Thaw in the fridge and reheat on a skillet before serving.

french-or-catalina-dressing-fat-free.title: French or Catalina Dressing, Fat Free

content.title: About
content.content: French and Catalina fat‑free dressings are low‑calorie sauces made from tomato puree, vinegar, spices and aromatic herbs. They contain no added oil, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Both dressings are popular in the United States as alternatives to traditional mayo‑based sauces.
Catalina dressing often includes pineapple juice, giving it a sweet‑tart flavor.
French dressing is typically enriched with mustard and herbs such as oregano and basil.
The fat‑free version reduces calories to about 15–20 kcal per 100 ml.
These sauces are commonly used on salads, as marinades, and as dips.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: The absence of fat makes the dressing suitable for weight‑management.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Tomato juice and vinegar provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes offers antioxidant protection.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Vinegar stimulates gastric juice production, aiding digestion.

items.title: Reduced sodium
items.content: Fat‑free versions typically contain less salt than traditional sauces.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some formulations may contain mustard, soy sauce or pineapple, which can trigger allergies.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The high acidity of vinegar may irritate the stomach in people with gastritis.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Catalina dressing is sometimes sweetened, which may be a concern for diabetics.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Drizzle over salads, use as a marinade for chicken or fish, serve with vegetable sticks, or as a dip for appetizers. Pairs well with leafy greens, grilled vegetables and seafood.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated after opening in a tightly sealed bottle. Once opened, it is best used within 1–2 weeks. Discard if the smell, color or taste changes.

pizza-cheese-from-school-lunch-thin-crus.title: Cheese Pizza, School Lunch, Thin Crust

content.title: About
content.content: Thin‑crust cheese pizza served in school cafeterias is a dish made from leavened wheat dough topped with tomato sauce and melted cheese. The dough is prepared with flour, water, yeast and a pinch of salt, and after baking it becomes crisp and light. The pizza provides carbohydrates, protein and calcium as part of a balanced school meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thin crust allows faster baking in large batches, which is ideal for school kitchens.
The cheese used is often a blend of mozzarella and processed cheese to keep costs low.
Serving pizza in schools became popular in the 1990s as part of nutrition diversification programs.
School pizza sauce is usually made without added sugar to reduce calorie content.
A thin crust contains fewer calories than a traditional thick crust, making it more suitable for children’s diets.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Cheese supplies a substantial amount of calcium, essential for bone growth in children.

items.title: Good protein content
items.content: Both the dough and cheese provide a mix of plant‑based and dairy proteins that support tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tomatoes and yeast‑leavened dough contain vitamins B1, B2 and B6, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Lower fat level
items.content: The thin crust and moderate cheese amount make this pizza less fatty than traditional versions.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Children with lactose intolerance or milk‑protein allergy may react to the cheese.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheese and sauce can contain added salt, so sodium intake should be monitored.

items.title: Gluten in the dough
items.content: Standard wheat dough contains gluten, which is a concern for children with celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Even with a thin crust, a serving can be calorie‑dense if eaten in large portions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut the pizza into bite‑size slices and serve warm. Adding fresh vegetables such as tomatoes or cucumber, or a sprinkle of herbs, can boost nutritional value. A light dusting of oregano is optional.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in an oven or microwave to keep the crust crisp.

tuna-noodle-casserole-with-vegetables-cr.title: Tuna Noodle Casserole with Vegetables and Cream Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Tuna noodle casserole with vegetables in a cream (or white) sauce is a baked dish that combines cooked noodles, chunks of tuna, mixed vegetables (such as peas, carrots, broccoli) and a smooth sauce made from cream or milk. The dish is popular in American home cooking as a quick, hearty family meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canned tuna is commonly used in casseroles because it stores well and has a mild flavor.
The classic recipe appeared in the United States in the mid‑20th century when canned tuna became widely affordable.
The cream sauce is usually made from milk, cream, flour, and cheese, giving the casserole a rich texture.
Variations may replace noodles with rice, quinoa, or gluten‑free pasta for a healthier twist.
Casserole portions are often cut into squares, making them convenient for school lunches and picnics.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Tuna provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Canned tuna contains EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tuna and dairy ingredients supply B12, B6, and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Vegetables add fiber and micronutrients
items.content: Added vegetables increase dietary fiber, vitamin A, vitamin C, and potassium.

items.title: Calcium from dairy
items.content: Cream and cheese enrich the dish with calcium for bone health.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned tuna often contains added salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Tuna can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: The cream sauce adds saturated fat; a lighter milk‑based sauce can be used as an alternative.

items.title: Mercury in tuna
items.content: While mercury levels in canned tuna are generally low, pregnant women and children should limit consumption.

content.title: How to Prepare and Serve
content.content: Cook the noodles until al dente, combine with tuna, cooked vegetables, and cream sauce. Transfer to a baking dish, top with shredded cheese, and bake 20‑25 minutes at 180 °C (350 °F) until golden. Serve hot, garnished with fresh parsley or chives.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the casserole to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in the microwave or oven to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F) before serving.
